paragraphs: Federated bilevel learning involves two connected optimization problems distributed across clients. The paper addresses a difficult combination: clients have differently distributed data, and only some clients participate in each round. Previous approaches left open whether increasing participation could provide a provable linear improvement in convergence under this data heterogeneity.

The proposed algorithm, FedMBO, introduces a client sampling scheme for estimating the hypergradient, the quantity used to update the outer optimization problem. This makes sampling part of the optimization design itself. The analysis explicitly accounts for both the number of participating clients and the total number of iterations.

The stated convergence rate is O(1/√(nK) + 1/K + √n/K^(3/2)), where n denotes participating clients and K denotes iterations. The authors establish the first theoretical linear speedup result for non-identically distributed federated bilevel optimization. The full expression also shows that convergence has several contributing terms, rather than depending on participation alone. Experiments support the theoretical results and demonstrate the method’s effectiveness.
icml-2023-achieving-linear-speedup-in-no.tldr: FedMBO establishes theoretical linear speedup for federated bilevel optimization with heterogeneous data and partial client participation.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student network using information from a teacher. This paper asks which teachers work well for small-kernel convolutional networks, which are attractive for resource-limited applications. Transferring knowledge from Transformers has previously been less effective, with architectural differences suggested as a reason.

The authors study large-kernel convolutional networks as teachers and find them substantially more effective for these students. Their architectural similarity offers a route for transferring useful information between the networks. Experiments cover distillation through both output predictions and internal features, using existing methods without specialized changes to architecture or training recipes.

The study reports a pure convolutional model with fewer than 30 million parameters reaching 83.1% top-1 ImageNet accuracy, outperforming the named contemporary methods in the abstract. It also finds that students can inherit characteristics such as larger effective receptive fields. These results make teacher compatibility an important part of the distillation story: the tested large-kernel teachers help compact students acquire useful properties while retaining a convolutional architecture.
icml-2023-are-large-kernels-better-teach.tldr: Large-kernel convolutional networks prove more effective than Transformers as teachers for small-kernel ConvNets in the reported distillation experiments.

paragraphs: Bandit learners make decisions using limited feedback, and delayed feedback makes those decisions harder because recent outcomes may still be unavailable. This paper introduces Banker Online Mirror Descent, a framework that extends online mirror descent to handle such delays. Its central contribution is to almost separate delay management from the design choices specific to a learning task.

The framework provides a general route to regret bounds that scale like √T + √D, ignoring logarithmic factors. Here, T counts decision rounds and D measures total feedback delay. Regret expresses the learner’s accumulated disadvantage relative to a benchmark, so this form describes how the cost of learning grows with both time and delayed information.

The authors apply the framework to scale-free adversarial multi-armed bandits and adversarial linear bandits, obtaining the first stated bounds of their respective forms. The first application also yields a result without delays: its regret matches the corresponding lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Thus, the framework contributes both a reusable treatment of delays and an improvement for an ordinary, non-delayed bandit setting.
icml-2023-banker-online-mirror-descent-a.tldr: Banker-OMD largely separates feedback-delay handling from bandit algorithm design while delivering improved regret guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper studies decisions in which a learner selects a subset of available options each round and receives feedback about those selected options. Each option has features, but the relationship between those features and its score is unknown. Neural networks approximate this relationship, allowing the learning model to represent complex score functions.

The authors develop Combinatorial Neural UCB and Combinatorial Neural Thompson Sampling. Both combine neural score estimation with exploration. For the Thompson sampling approach, they adapt an optimistic sampling technique so that optimism applies to the selected combination, addressing the fact that a decision contains several options together.

The paper proves regret guarantees for both algorithms, with bounds depending on the time horizon, a neural tangent kernel’s effective dimension, and, in some expressions, the subset size. The authors identify these as the first combinatorial neural bandit methods with regret guarantees, to their knowledge. They also establish a first worst-case Thompson sampling guarantee for the general contextual combinatorial setting. Numerical experiments report superior performance for the proposed algorithms.
icml-2023-combinatorial-neural-bandits-a.tldr: Two neural bandit algorithms learn to select combinations of options while providing theoretical regret guarantees.

paragraphs: The loss function tells a classifier how to evaluate its mistakes during training. Cross-entropy is the usual choice, but this paper investigates whether combining it with a square-loss component improves results. The proposed loss, called squentropy, adds cross-entropy to the average square loss over the incorrect classes.

This construction retains the familiar classification objective while also penalizing scores assigned to wrong classes through the additional term. In extensive multiclass experiments, squentropy achieves better classification accuracy than either cross-entropy alone or a rescaled square loss. The authors also report better calibration, meaning that confidence estimates better reflect prediction correctness, and lower variation across random initializations.

The practical appeal is that multiclass squentropy introduces no extra parameters requiring adjustment. It can also frequently use the same optimization settings, including learning rate, as cross-entropy. That makes it a potentially convenient replacement within an existing training setup. The evidence supports improvements across the reported experiments, while the ability to reuse training settings is explicitly frequent rather than guaranteed for every model.
icml-2023-cut-your-losses-with-squentrop.tldr: Squentropy combines cross-entropy with a penalty on incorrect classes, improving accuracy, calibration, and initialization stability in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes data into nested groups. This paper studies how closely a private algorithm can approximate a formal hierarchical clustering objective while satisfying differential privacy. It develops both impossibility results and algorithms, connecting the privacy requirement to the quality of the resulting hierarchy.

For general inputs, the authors establish a lower bound on unavoidable additive error that depends on dataset size and privacy strength. They then provide a polynomial-time approximation algorithm with a larger additive error and an exponential-time algorithm that meets the lower bound. Together, these results distinguish what privacy fundamentally costs from what their computationally efficient method achieves.

The paper also studies the stochastic block model, a structured model of graphs. Under a separation assumption on its blocks, the authors obtain a private approximation factor approaching one and recover the blocks exactly. This stronger result depends on the stated graph structure and separation condition. An empirical study validates the proposed algorithms’ performance, complementing the theoretical account of general inputs and the more favorable structured setting.
icml-2023-differentially-private-hierarc.tldr: The paper bounds the cost of private hierarchical clustering and gives stronger guarantees for sufficiently separated stochastic block models.

paragraphs: Clustering distributed data becomes harder when some points are treated as outliers. Earlier distributed k-center methods required quadratic local running time and communication that depended on the dataset’s aspect ratio. This paper introduces sampling strategies intended to reduce computation and communication while retaining approximation guarantees.

The first strategy, inliers-recalling sampling, avoids guessing the optimal clustering radius. It uses four communication rounds, has local running time linear in data size, and removes aspect-ratio dependence from communication. The second, space-narrowing sampling, adapts sample sizes to the distribution of outliers on each machine. It uses two rounds and has communication cost independent of the number of outliers.

Both k-center methods provide a bicriteria guarantee: they approximate clustering quality while allowing a controlled increase in the outlier budget. The methods also extend to k-median and k-means with outliers when points are randomly partitioned across machines. That partition assumption qualifies the extension. Experiments suggest that the proposed two-round algorithms outperform other state-of-the-art methods, supporting their practical promise alongside the formal guarantees.
icml-2023-fast-algorithms-for-distribute.tldr: Adaptive sampling reduces distributed clustering costs while preserving bicriteria approximation guarantees for handling outliers.

paragraphs: Federated contextual bandits combine learning across clients with repeated decisions informed by contextual features. This paper asks how much learning performance must suffer when privacy protects an entire user’s contribution. It introduces a common framework for defining privacy in this sequential setting and studies both central and local differential privacy.

For central privacy, the authors propose an algorithm called ROBIN. They derive upper and lower regret bounds that nearly match in their dependence on the number of clients and the privacy budget. This establishes near-optimality with respect to those quantities: the algorithm’s dependence is close to what the accompanying lower bounds permit.

For local privacy, the paper instead establishes several lower bounds on the additional regret required. Under different conditions, the blow-up is at least min{1/ε, M} or min{1/√ε, √M}, where M is the client count and ε is the privacy budget. These are conditional alternatives, not a single universal formula. The results make the learning cost of different user-level privacy definitions mathematically explicit.
icml-2023-federated-linear-contextual-ba.tldr: ROBIN nearly matches central user-level privacy regret limits, while lower bounds reveal conditional performance costs under local privacy.

paragraphs: An agent may observe the same environment through several sources, each providing a different view. Multi-view reinforcement learning aims to combine these observations to choose effective actions. The challenge goes beyond summarizing several inputs: observations depend on one another over time, and some sources may intermittently disappear.

Fuse2Control, or F2C, uses an information-theoretic approach to learn an underlying state space model from sequences of these observations. Its focus is the information relevant to control. Learning from sequences addresses the temporal structure that makes direct application of ordinary multi-view representation methods difficult.

Across experiments on several control tasks, the authors report that F2C effectively combines task-relevant information from many views. They also report linear scaling with the number of views and robustness to arbitrary missing-view scenarios. These findings support the approach as a way to combine multiple observation streams without requiring every stream to remain continuously available. The contribution connects representation learning to the needs of an acting agent, with empirical evidence covering both aggregation and missing observations.
icml-2023-information-theoretic-state-sp.tldr: Fuse2Control learns control-relevant state models from multiple observation streams, with reported linear scaling and robustness to missing views.

paragraphs: Combinatorial generalization means assembling familiar attributes into combinations that were not previously experienced. Earlier unsupervised approaches often pursued this through disentangled representations, attempting to separate attributes within a representation. The paper is motivated by findings that such separation alone is insufficient and may not correlate with successful recombination.

MAGANet instead learns transformations between pairs of examples by modeling a group action. The central object of learning is therefore how one example changes into another. This places the structure of transformations at the center of generation, providing a different approach to producing unfamiliar combinations under distribution shift.

The authors evaluate this ability in two settings called Recombination-to-Element and Recombination-to-Range. Their experiments report stronger generalization in both quantitative and qualitative assessments, together with better generated images than traditional models. The stated findings support learning transformations as a useful route to combinatorial generation in the tested settings. They do not make disentanglement a sufficient condition; the paper’s motivation is precisely that representing attributes separately does not by itself establish an ability to recombine them.
icml-2023-maganet-achieving-combinatoria.tldr: MAGANet learns transformations between examples to generate unfamiliar attribute combinations, improving generalization in two reported evaluation settings.

paragraphs: Generating audio from text faces two obstacles highlighted by this paper: limited high-quality paired text and audio, and the difficulty of modeling long continuous sound signals. Make-An-Audio addresses both within a diffusion-based generation system. Its design combines a strategy for expanding useful prompt information with a more manageable representation of audio.

The first component creates enhanced pseudo prompts through a distill-then-reprogram procedure, making use of audio without accompanying language. This alleviates paired-data scarcity by enabling many concept compositions. The second uses a spectrogram autoencoder so that generation predicts a learned audio representation instead of directly predicting waveforms. Contrastive language-audio pretraining supplies representations connecting language and sound.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on both objective and subjective benchmark evaluations. They also demonstrate controllability and generalization beyond text-conditioned generation through an X-to-Audio capability described as accepting user-defined input modalities. Together, the findings support combining prompt enhancement and representation-based generation to improve audio synthesis, while the reported broader-input demonstrations extend the system’s stated scope beyond text prompts.
icml-2023-make-an-audio-text-to-audio-ge.tldr: Make-An-Audio combines pseudo-prompt enhancement and learned audio representations to improve diffusion-based audio generation.

paragraphs: Physics-constrained neural solvers learn to solve partial differential equations while respecting physical equations during training. Their constraints must resolve small-scale physics to maintain simulation accuracy and stability. That requirement can produce large inputs, outputs, and networks, making the solver expensive even when neural methods are intended to accelerate computation.

NeuralStagger divides the original learning problem across space and time into several coarser-resolution subtasks. Each subtask receives its own smaller neural solver. The outputs are arranged to reconstruct the original solution, and the solvers are trained jointly using the original physics-constrained loss. This retains the full solution as the object on which the physical constraints are enforced.

Because the component solvers can run in parallel, the approach can achieve solution speed comparable to a coarse-resolution solver. The trained components also permit simulation at multiple resolutions. Experiments on two- and three-dimensional fluid dynamics report an additional 10–100-fold speedup. The authors further show that the learned model can be used for optimal control, extending the demonstrated utility beyond simulation alone.
icml-2023-neuralstagger-accelerating-phy.tldr: NeuralStagger combines parallel coarse-resolution neural solvers into a physics-constrained solution, reporting 10–100-fold additional speedups in fluid simulations.

paragraphs: A coreset is a compact substitute for a larger dataset that approximately preserves clustering costs for any choice of centers. For k-median, this means a small representation can support comparison of candidate center sets. This paper investigates how small such representations can be when the data lives in a low-dimensional Euclidean space.

Much previous work emphasized guarantees that do not depend on dimension, especially for high-dimensional data. The authors ask whether knowing the dimension is small allows substantially better bounds. They answer affirmatively for a range of parameter settings and also prove new lower bounds, identifying limits on how far compression can go.

For one-dimensional k-median, the paper settles coreset size up to logarithmic factors. A particularly notable consequence is a strong separation between the one-center and two-center problems on a line. This means that allowing just one additional center can materially change the coreset-size requirement. The authors identify it as the first known separation of this kind between one and two centers in any dimension.
icml-2023-on-coresets-for-clustering-in-.tldr: Low-dimensional k-median admits improved coreset bounds, with the one-dimensional case settled up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: This paper studies causal models in which a cause changes both the expected effect and the size of its noise. The model is Y = f(X) + g(X)N, with noise N independent of X and a positive scaling function g. This permits heteroscedasticity: the amount of variability can depend on the cause.

The authors show that causal direction is identifiable within this model class except for some pathological cases. They then propose two estimators to test these findings empirically. One uses nonlinear feature maps and the other uses neural networks. Both describe the conditional distribution of the effect as a Gaussian expressed through its natural parameters.

When the feature maps are correctly specified, the authors prove joint concavity for the estimation formulation and consistency for identifying cause and effect. Those guarantees do not transfer to the neural estimator. Its advantage is flexibility in fitting functions of arbitrary complexity, and it achieves state-of-the-art benchmark performance. The paper thus separates a conditional theoretical guarantee from the empirical benefits of a more expressive estimator.
icml-2023-on-the-identifiability-and-est.tldr: Location-scale noise models can identify causal direction except in pathological cases, with separate theoretical and empirical results for two estimators.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction produces sets of possible outcomes with a desired coverage level, giving a way to express uncertainty around predictions. This paper brings that capability to one-shot federated learning, where data remains distributed and communication is restricted to a single round. The main question is whether useful coverage guarantees can survive that communication constraint.

The proposed method uses a quantile-of-quantiles estimator. Its central idea is to construct the quantity needed for prediction sets through quantile information from the distributed setting. The authors prove that prediction sets with the desired coverage can be computed in one communication round for any distribution. They also describe a locally differentially private version to mitigate privacy concerns.

Across a broad collection of experiments, the resulting sets have coverage and length very similar to those obtained centrally. Both properties matter: coverage measures whether the sets include the outcome at the intended frequency, while length describes their breadth. The findings support one-shot federation as a practical setting for uncertainty-aware prediction, alongside the paper’s distribution-free coverage result.
icml-2023-one-shot-federated-conformal-p.tldr: A quantile-of-quantiles estimator enables federated conformal prediction with desired coverage in one communication round.

paragraphs: Adversarial imitation learning uses a discriminator to distinguish an agent’s behavior from expert behavior, then uses that distinction to guide learning. This paper identifies poor discriminator representations as a major source of difficulty on challenging tasks. Binary classification can separate examples without providing a meaningful measure of how behavior should improve.

Policy Contrastive Imitation Learning, or PCIL, learns a representation space anchored on different policies. It then defines a smooth reward using cosine similarity within that space. The aim is to make behavioral comparisons more informative, so that the reward encourages imitation through the learned structure of policies rather than relying solely on a binary decision.

The authors interpret the representation objective as a stronger version of the adversarial imitation objective and establish its validity through the apprenticeship learning framework. Experiments on the DeepMind Control suite show that PCIL can reach state-of-the-art performance. Qualitative results additionally suggest a smoother, more meaningful representation space. Those visual or qualitative findings support the proposed explanation of the method’s behavior without establishing it as a universal outcome.
icml-2023-policy-contrastive-imitation-l.tldr: PCIL uses policy-based contrastive representations and a smooth similarity reward to improve imitation learning.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning in high-dimensional continuous action spaces requires a policy capable of representing useful choices. This paper targets limitations of the commonly used Gaussian parameterization by developing a multimodal policy. Such a policy can represent distinct possibilities within the agent’s behavior rather than relying on a single Gaussian form.

The framework treats the policy as a generative model of optimal trajectories and conditions it on a latent variable. From this construction, the authors derive a variational optimization objective that promotes exploration. Their practical algorithm, Reparameterized Policy Gradient, combines this policy parameterization with a learned world model to support exploration and data-efficient learning.

Experiments show that the approach can help agents escape local optima in tasks with dense rewards. For difficult sparse-reward environments, the reported success includes an object-centric intrinsic reward, so that component is part of the stated result. The method consistently outperforms previous approaches across the tested tasks. Together, these findings support the combination of multimodal policies and model-based learning as a useful approach to exploring different possible trajectories.
icml-2023-reparameterized-policy-learnin.tldr: Reparameterized Policy Gradient combines latent-conditioned multimodal policies with a learned world model to improve exploration and data efficiency.

paragraphs: Integer linear programs express many combinatorial optimization problems, but finding strong solutions quickly depends on the search strategy. Large Neighborhood Search improves solutions by exploring substantial changes around a current candidate. Its effectiveness depends on the heuristic guiding that exploration, and choosing such heuristics remains a central challenge.

CL-LNS learns a faster heuristic from an expert heuristic that is expensive to compute. It gathers both positive and negative solution samples and uses contrastive learning to distinguish useful examples from less useful ones. Graph attention networks and a richer feature set further improve the learned method’s performance.

The authors report state-of-the-art anytime performance on several integer programming benchmarks. Anytime performance concerns the quality of solutions available as computation proceeds, making it relevant when optimization may be stopped at different times. The reported evaluation includes primal gap, primal integral, survival rates, and best-performing rate. The contribution is an empirical demonstration that guidance from a costly expert can be converted into a more efficient learned search heuristic with strong performance across those benchmarks.
icml-2023-searching-large-neighborhoods-.tldr: CL-LNS learns an efficient integer-program search heuristic from positive and negative examples supplied by a costly expert.

paragraphs: High-rate sensor streams can contain many measurements that are difficult to inspect directly. Deep learning can compress those measurements, but the resulting latent representations may still be hard to interpret. SOM-CPC addresses this gap by seeking a representation that supports an organized two-dimensional visualization while preserving information from higher dimensions.

The model combines unsupervised contrastive learning with self-organizing maps. Its purpose is to make the structure of high-rate time series easier to examine, rather than treating dimensionality reduction alone as sufficient for understanding. The paper focuses on this challenging setting across both synthetic data and real recordings.

The evaluation includes physiological signals and audio. The authors report that SOM-CPC outperforms strong alternatives, including deep feature extraction followed by conventional dimensionality reduction and models that jointly train a deep network with a self-organizing map. These comparisons support the usefulness of the proposed combination for the tested data. The broader implication is a promising way to study latent patterns in continuous streams, with improved understanding presented as potential rather than as a guaranteed outcome of every visualization.
icml-2023-som-cpc-unsupervised-contrasti.tldr: SOM-CPC combines contrastive learning and self-organizing maps to create structured two-dimensional representations of high-rate time series.

paragraphs: Hyperparameters strongly influence neural network performance, but selecting them often requires manual effort. Bayesian model selection with a Laplace approximation provides a way to optimize them using gradients on training data. The scalability problem addressed here is that previous estimators require a full dataset pass for each hyperparameter gradient.

The authors introduce lower bounds on the linearized Laplace approximation to marginal likelihood. These bounds support stochastic gradient optimization, providing a way to estimate useful updates without the same full-data requirement. Their derivation uses a function-space formulation that can be estimated through the neural tangent kernel.

The resulting estimators allow a tradeoff between estimation accuracy and computational cost. This matters because the objective being optimized is already an approximation, and the method explicitly exposes another computational choice within its estimation. Experiments show that the proposed estimators can substantially accelerate gradient-based hyperparameter optimization. The contribution is therefore a more scalable way to use Bayesian selection objectives, supported by empirical speed improvements rather than a claim that every hyperparameter search becomes faster.
icml-2023-stochastic-marginal-likelihood.tldr: Neural tangent kernel-based bounds enable stochastic hyperparameter optimization and can substantially reduce its computational cost.

paragraphs: Vector quantization represents learned embeddings using entries from a codebook. Training networks with this discrete operation often relies on straight-through estimation to approximate gradients. This paper investigates why that training can become unstable and identifies a mismatch between the distribution of model embeddings and the distribution of code vectors as the main cause.

The analysis points to sparse codebook gradients and an asymmetric commitment loss as contributing factors. These can leave code-vector assignments poorly aligned with the embeddings they represent. The authors propose an affine reparameterization of code vectors, alternating optimization to reduce straight-through gradient error, and a revised commitment loss to improve alignment.

Together, these changes aim to improve the approximation underlying the gradient estimator and ultimately improve model performance. The authors demonstrate their effectiveness with AlexNet, ResNet, and Vision Transformer architectures on image classification and generative modeling tasks. The contribution connects a specific diagnosis of optimization instability to several targeted training changes, with evidence spanning multiple architectures and tasks rather than a single model configuration.
icml-2023-straightening-out-the-straight.tldr: Aligning embeddings and code vectors improves straight-through optimization and performance in vector-quantized neural networks.

paragraphs: When several agents learn together, their behavior may continue changing rather than settle at an equilibrium. Previous understanding often relied on special game classes where convergence could be established. This paper studies smooth Q-learning to examine what exploration does in broader network games, including those with complex, nonconvergent dynamics.

The authors show that exploration brings Q-learning into a neighborhood of an equilibrium in any network game. This does not require the dynamics to reach the equilibrium itself. Increasing exploration shrinks that neighborhood and reduces the ability of all agents to improve their payoffs, giving a precise sense in which exploration improves convergence behavior.

That improvement can have a performance cost. For a broad class of games, the paper shows that social welfare decreases as exploration increases. Experiments suggest the same tradeoff is more general: stronger exploration improves convergence while reducing payoff performance. The findings distinguish being closer to equilibrium from achieving higher collective rewards, showing why a more stable learning process need not be the more rewarding one.
icml-2023-the-impact-of-exploration-on-c.tldr: Greater exploration brings multi-agent Q-learning closer to equilibrium but can reduce collective payoff performance.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much of a dataset must be examined to approximately solve k-median clustering. It relates that query requirement to a dataset property called balancedness, denoted β, where one represents perfect balance. The goal is to understand when a simple uniform sample can provide enough information for accurate clustering.

The authors prove that any algorithm needs at least order 1/β queries to obtain a constant-factor approximation. They also show that a uniform sample whose size is polynomial in k, inverse accuracy tolerance, and inverse balancedness suffices for a near-exact approximation in various metric spaces. The sampling guarantee nearly matches the lower bound, according to the paper.

The lower bound also implies that existing coreset constructions cannot be query-efficient in the sense studied. Experiments find that balancedness is usually well bounded in many real datasets and that uniform sampling performs consistently well in the examined settings. These results support uniform sampling as a viable clustering strategy while making dataset balance an explicit part of its theoretical explanation.
icml-2023-the-power-of-uniform-sampling-.tldr: Dataset balancedness explains when uniform sampling can approximate k-median with nearly optimal query requirements.

paragraphs: A network community profile describes how the quality of clusters changes with their size. This paper connects that profile to μ-conductance, a measure originating in work on Markov chains for sampling convex bodies. Like ordinary graph conductance, it concerns how well groups are separated, but it excludes sets with small volume.

The authors derive a sequence of optimization problems, including a low-rank semidefinite program, that produces a lower bound on the optimal μ-conductance value. This supplies a mathematical bound on community structure across a range of sizes. It complements searching for good clusters by establishing limits on how good the relevant optimum can be.

The paper presents these as the first theoretically sound bounds on network community profile behavior over a wide range of cluster sizes. Its algorithm scales to graphs with hundreds of thousands of nodes. Demonstrations on real-world graphs show how the framework can validate predicted structures. The contribution therefore joins a theoretical connection between two measures with a computational method large enough to examine substantial networks.
icml-2023-theoretical-bounds-on-the-netw.tldr: Low-rank semidefinite optimization provides theoretical bounds on community quality across cluster sizes in large networks.

paragraphs: Some datasets contain both missing entries and observed counts that systematically fall below the true totals. This paper studies that combination in multi-aspect data represented as tensors. The motivating problem includes estimating unobserved disease counts from neighboring regions whose recorded counts are themselves incomplete.

The proposed model combines a low-rank Poisson tensor with an unknown nonlinear extractor of side information. A joint algorithm learns the tensor structure and a neural network, using attributes alongside the observed counts. The modeling task includes both completing missing data and accounting for the process that causes under-counting.

The authors prove that, under stated reasonable conditions, partial observations can support recovery of fully counted tensor entries and each entry’s under-counting probability. The guarantee is conditional, rather than a claim that arbitrary incomplete counts reveal their true totals. Simulations and real-data experiments corroborate the theoretical claims. The authors identify this as the first theoretical support for under-counted multi-aspect completion, offering an explanation of when recovery is possible alongside an algorithm for performing it.
icml-2023-under-counted-tensor-completio.tldr: A joint tensor and neural model can recover missing true counts and under-counting probabilities under the paper’s theoretical conditions.
